PRIVATE, LOCAL-FIRST WORKFLOW

Find a duplicate vendor payment before you write it off.

Upload your accounts-payable payment history as a CSV and get a short list of likely double payments to review — the same kind of check a duplicate-payment recovery audit firm sells, run yourself, for free, on files that never leave your browser.

1. Payment ledger CSV

Needs a vendor, amount, and date column. Common names like vendor, amount, and payment_date work automatically. An invoice_number or similar reference column is optional but sharpens the check.

No export handy? — an eleven-row ledger carrying one of each thing this tool looks for.

Two payments to the same vendor, for the same amount, landing within this many days of each other are flagged for review even with no invoice-number match.

Review queue

Every row is a lead to verify against your vendor statement or your accounting system, not a determination that a payment was a duplicate or that any wrongdoing occurred.

Common questions

What counts as a likely duplicate payment here?

Three patterns: the same vendor and invoice number paid twice for the same amount (an exact duplicate submission), the same vendor and invoice number paid twice at different amounts (a possible partial payment or data-entry error), and the same vendor and amount paid under two invoice numbers that are nearly identical or that land close together in time. Each flagged pair says which pattern matched and why.

Will this flag legitimate recurring payments as duplicates?

It can, and it says so on that specific row. Rent, subscriptions, and retainers are the same vendor and the same amount by design, which is exactly the pattern the same-amount/near-date check looks for. Those rows are labeled "review", the lowest confidence tier, and the tool tells you to check whether the vendor is paid this amount on a regular schedule before treating it as a duplicate. The higher-confidence tiers (an exact invoice-number match, or two invoice numbers that look like a typo of each other) are far less likely to be a legitimate recurring charge, because a real recurring bill is issued under a new invoice number each cycle.

Does this submit a refund request or contact my vendor?

No. It only reads the CSV you choose and produces a list of pairs to review, plus a downloadable CSV of the same list. It does not contact a vendor, file a dispute, request a credit, or take any action on your behalf — you decide what to do with each flagged pair.

Is this the same as hiring a duplicate-payment recovery audit firm?

No. Recovery-audit firms typically work large enterprise AP ledgers on a contingency fee, taking a cut of whatever they help recover. This is a free, one-time, self-serve check of a CSV you already have, aimed at businesses too small for that kind of engagement. It finds candidates for you to verify yourself; it does not investigate, negotiate, or recover anything.

What columns does my CSV need?

A vendor name, a payment amount, and a payment date, using common header names such as vendor, amount, and date (payment_date, paid_date, and similar variants are also recognized). An invoice or reference number column sharpens the check considerably but is optional.

What if my export doesn't have an invoice number column?

The tool still runs, using only the same-vendor, same-amount, near-date check, and says so in the results. Add an invoice or reference column to your export if your accounting system can include one — it is what makes the exact-duplicate and near-duplicate-invoice checks possible.

Are my payment records uploaded anywhere?

No. Everything runs in your browser; the CSV never leaves your device. The optional usage counter records only that a check ran, not any vendor names, amounts, dates, or file contents.

Already checking your export by sorting a spreadsheet and scanning for repeats? See how this tool differs from a manual spreadsheet check — it catches an invoice-number typo and a payment weeks apart that a vendor sort would not.

Already considering a full recovery audit from a firm like PRGX? See how this one-time CSV check differs from PRGX's contingency-fee audit across an entire company's supplier spend.

Wondering why a payment gets flagged even when the amount doesn't match? See why the same invoice number at two different amounts still gets flagged for a worked example.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Duplicate payment audit

This tool vs. a spreadsheet

Most small businesses already look for duplicate payments the same way: export the AP history, sort by vendor, and scan for two rows that look alike. That catches the easiest case — the same vendor, same amount, same invoice number, a few rows apart. It is much weaker at the cases that actually cost money: a re-entered invoice number with one digit changed, a resubmission that lands weeks later instead of days, or telling a real duplicate apart from a rent payment that is supposed to repeat.

QuestionWhere to answer it
The same vendor and invoice number, paid twice, right next to each other after a sort? Either — a spreadsheet sort finds this fine.
Same vendor and amount, but the invoice number was re-typed with one digit off? This tool — it measures the edit distance between invoice numbers and flags a likely re-entry a sort would scatter across the sheet.
The same bill paid twice, three weeks apart, under a different reference? This tool — groups by vendor and amount across the whole export, not by adjacency after a sort, and reports the gap in days.
Is this flagged pair an actual duplicate, or just my recurring rent? This tool's confidence tiers — an invoice-number match is high confidence, a same-amount/near-date match with no invoice link is labeled “review” and says so explicitly.
Building and maintaining the sort, filters, and formulas myself? A spreadsheet — and re-doing it by hand every time you want to check a new export.
Is my payment data uploaded anywhere either way? No, on either — but this tool needs no formulas, no pivot table, and no manual re-sort to check the next export.
Check your AP export now

No account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the parsing and matching run in your browser, and your vendor names, amounts, dates, and the file itself stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Can't I just sort my AP export by vendor and scan for repeats?

Sorting by vendor finds the easy case: the same vendor, the same amount, the same invoice number, sitting a few rows apart. It does not find a duplicate that only looks different because of how it was re-entered — a typo'd invoice number, a payment recorded three weeks later under a new reference, or a partial-amount resubmission — because those rows sort next to entirely unrelated payments instead of next to each other. This tool runs three separate matching passes (exact invoice match, near-identical invoice numbers, and same-amount payments within a date window) across the whole export at once, so a duplicate that a vendor-sort would scatter across hundreds of rows still gets grouped and flagged.

Why is a typo'd invoice number hard to catch by eye in a spreadsheet?

INV-40219 and INV-40129 look identical at a glance in a column of a few hundred rows, and a plain vendor sort places them wherever their own invoice number falls — not next to each other. Catching that by eye means noticing a one-character difference in a string you were not specifically looking for. This tool measures the edit distance between invoice numbers within the same vendor and amount, and flags anything within two characters of another payment as a likely re-entry of the same bill, whether or not the two rows happen to be near each other.

How does this avoid flagging my rent or a subscription as a duplicate?

It does not avoid it entirely -- a genuine duplicate and a recurring charge can look identical from amount and vendor alone -- but it does not treat them the same way. An exact invoice-number match or a near-identical invoice number is high confidence, because a real recurring bill is issued under a new invoice number each cycle. A same-amount payment with no invoice link at all, landing within your chosen date window, is labeled "review" and says explicitly to check whether that vendor is paid this amount on a regular schedule before treating it as anything else. A spreadsheet sort returns the same rows either way, with no confidence tier to tell you which is which.

Does this replace the AP ledger or spreadsheet I already keep?

No. An ongoing ledger that tracks every vendor and every payment over months or years is still the right place to keep that record. This is a one-time check you run against an export from it — did any of these payments go out twice — and it keeps no copy of your data once you close the tab.

Weighing a full AP automation platform instead? See this tool vs. BILL (Bill.com). Considering a contingency recovery-audit firm? See this tool vs. PRGX.

It does not determine that any payment was fraudulent, wrongful, or actually duplicated — it flags statistical patterns in your own data for your review. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output against your vendor statements and accounting records before requesting a refund, credit, or correction from anyone. ← Duplicate payment audit

This tool vs. BILL (Bill.com)

BILL (formerly Bill.com) is an accounts-payable automation platform. Bills are captured into it, routed for approval, paid through it, and synced back to an accounting system, and a duplicate warning is one control inside that ongoing workflow. It is a process: adopting it changes how your payables run, month after month.

This page is not a process and does not want to be. It answers one retrospective question about payments you have already made: did any of these go out twice — read from a CSV export in your browser, with nothing uploaded, nothing migrated, and nothing to subscribe to.

Is this flagged pair actually a duplicate, or is it our monthly rent? This tool's confidence tiers — the same-amount/near-date tier is labelled “review” and says outright that recurring charges match it too.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or BILL?

They operate at different scopes. BILL is an accounts-payable automation platform: bills are captured into it, routed for approval, paid through it, and synced back to an accounting system, and duplicate warnings are one control inside that ongoing workflow. Adopting it means moving how your AP process runs. This page does not run your AP process and never will. It reads one CSV export of payments you have already made, in your browser, and returns a short reviewed list of likely double payments with the reason each pair matched. If your AP already runs on a platform, this is a second opinion over its output; if it does not, this is a check you can do this afternoon without changing anything.

Can I check for duplicate payments without moving my AP process onto a platform?

Yes, and that is the specific gap this page exists to close. Platform duplicate warnings are preventive: they fire while a bill is being entered, inside the system the bill was entered into. That does nothing about payments already made, payments made outside the platform, or the period before you adopted one. A CSV export of payment history is something almost every accounting system can produce, and checking it needs no migration, no subscription, and no per-user seats — you export, you check, you keep the review list.

Does this see duplicates a platform's own control would have missed?

Sometimes, because it looks at a different thing. A preventive control compares a bill being entered against bills already in that system. This runs four retrospective checks across the whole export at once: the same vendor and invoice number paid twice for the same amount, the same vendor and invoice number paid twice at different amounts, the same vendor and amount under invoice numbers that are a likely typo of each other, and the same vendor and amount landing within a date window you set. The last tier is labelled “review” rather than “duplicate”, because rent, subscriptions, and retainers match that pattern by design. Nothing here proves a payment was duplicated — it produces candidates for you to verify against your vendor statements.

vs-prgx.html.text:
← Duplicate payment audit

This tool vs. PRGX

PRGX is a recovery-audit firm: it reviews a client's accounts-payable transaction history for overpayments, duplicate payments, missed early-payment discounts, and pricing or tax errors, then helps recover what it finds. Engagements are typically self-funding or contingency-based — the fee comes out of what is actually recovered, and PRGX says no recovery means no payment is owed. PRGX's own materials describe roughly a third of the largest Fortune 500 companies as clients, which is the scale this kind of audit is built for: a data feed into PRGX's systems, a signed engagement, and a team reviewing the results across an entire enterprise's supplier spend.

That makes PRGX the right choice for a full recovery-audit engagement across an entire company's accounts-payable history, covering more than duplicate payments. This page answers a narrower, faster question: does this one CSV export contain likely duplicate vendor payments worth a closer look — with no engagement, no contract, and nothing uploaded.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or hire PRGX?

They serve different scales. That kind of engagement needs a data feed, a signed contract, and a team reviewing results, which is not realistic for a small business checking one export. This page is a free, one-time, self-serve check: choose a CSV, get a list of likely duplicate vendor payments to review yourself, with nothing uploaded and no engagement to set up.

Does PRGX only catch duplicate payments?

No — duplicate payments are one category among several. PRGX's published guides describe recovery audits also finding missed early-payment discounts, pricing and tax errors, and other under- or over-billing across a client's full supplier spend, not only exact or near-duplicate payments. This tool does the one thing its name says: it flags likely duplicate or double vendor payments in the CSV you give it. It does not check pricing terms, discount capture, or tax treatment.

This calculator has no engagement and no fee of any kind, contingent or otherwise. why-does-the-same-invoice-at-two-amounts.text:
← Duplicate payment audit

Why does the same invoice number at two different amounts get flagged?

Most people picture a duplicate payment as the exact same amount going out twice. It doesn't have to be. When the same vendor's invoice number shows up on two payments for different amounts, that is still worth a second look -- it just means something other than a clean, exact repeat, so this tool ranks it medium confidence and tells you what to check rather than calling it a duplicate outright.

Open the free duplicate payment audit

Worked example

This is the exact pattern in the tool's own bundled worked example (click "Load a worked example" on the calculator to see it):

VendorInvoiceDateAmount
Cascade Freight LinesINV-881202026-03-05$2,450.00
Cascade Freight LinesINV-881202026-03-09$245.00

Same vendor, same invoice number, four days apart -- but the second payment is exactly a tenth of the first. That specific ratio is a signature worth recognizing: a dropped decimal point or a mistyped digit produces exactly this kind of gap. The tool's own reasoning for this pair:

"Cascade Freight Lines: invoice INV-88120 was paid twice at different amounts ($2450.00 on 2026-03-05, $245.00 on 2026-03-09) — check for a partial payment or a data-entry error."

It does not tell you which one happened -- a genuine $245.00 partial payment and a $245.00 typo of a $2,450.00 bill produce the identical two rows in a CSV. Pulling the original invoice PDF is the only way to tell them apart.

Common questions

Why does the same invoice number at two different amounts get flagged at all?

Because the same vendor paying the same invoice number twice is unusual regardless of the amount -- a real invoice normally gets paid once. A different amount on the second payment means it is not a clean exact-duplicate (same invoice, same amount), so it is ranked medium confidence rather than high, and the tool tells you to check for a partial payment or a data-entry error rather than calling it a duplicate outright.

What does the worked example actually show?

Cascade Freight Lines' invoice INV-88120 was paid $2,450.00 on 2026-03-05, then paid again, same invoice number, at $245.00 on 2026-03-09. That tenfold difference is exactly the kind of gap a dropped decimal or a mistyped digit produces -- worth checking against the original bill before assuming either payment was correct.

Could this be a legitimate partial payment instead of an error?

Yes -- a vendor invoice split across two payments (a deposit and a balance, for example) will also produce this exact pattern: same invoice number, two different amounts. The tool cannot tell a legitimate installment apart from a duplicate paid at the wrong amount from the CSV alone, which is why this tier is medium confidence and says to check, not high confidence saying to refund.

How is this different from the exact-duplicate tier?

The exact-duplicate tier is the same vendor, same invoice number, and the same amount paid twice -- as clean a duplicate as a CSV can show, so it is ranked high confidence. This tier drops the amount match: same vendor and invoice number, but two different amounts, which could be a duplicate paid inconsistently, a partial payment, or a typo, so it is ranked one tier below and phrased as a question rather than a finding.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The CSV you check never leaves your browser -- there is no upload, no account, and no copy kept once you close the tab. Anonymous feature counts are local-only, contain no financial data, and can be turned off from the calculator's own page.
